title: The Shock Machine (Milgram, 1961)

youtube.title: Would You Shock a Stranger If a Man in a Lab Coat Told You To? #Shorts
youtube.description:
Yale, 1961. You answer a newspaper ad: $4 for one hour, in a "memory study". Then a man in a grey lab coat hands you a switch.

This is Stanley Milgram's famous obedience experiment, told from the inside. 65% of people went all the way to 450 volts. But the real lesson is in what happened when just two people said no.

Would YOU be the first to say no? Tell me in the comments.

Sources:
- Milgram, S. (1963). Behavioral Study of Obedience. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 67(4).
- Milgram, S. (1974). Obedience to Authority: An Experimental View.

sources: Milgram, S. (1963). Behavioral Study of Obedience. J Abnormal & Social Psychology 67(4): 65% (26 of 40) reached 450 V.
Milgram, S. (1974). Obedience to Authority: 'Two peers rebel' variation, about 1 in 10 went to the end.
Newspaper ad (New Haven Register): $4.00 for one hour of your time; memory study at Yale.
The learner was a confederate (actor); no real shocks were given.
lines: New Haven, 1961. A newspaper ad offers four dollars, for one hour of your time, in a memory study at Yale.
A man in a grey lab coat gives you a job. You're the teacher. The man in the next room is the learner.
Every wrong answer, you press a switch. Fifteen volts. Then thirty. All the way up to four hundred and fifty.
At a hundred and fifty volts, he cries out. He begs you to stop.
You turn around. The man in the coat says calmly: the experiment requires that you continue.
Experts expected almost no one to go to the end. Sixty-five percent did.
The shocks were fake. The learner was an actor. The only real thing in that room was you.
But when two other teachers refused, almost everyone refused too. Only about one in ten went all the way.
So maybe it isn't about how strong you are. It's about whether someone goes first. Would you be the first to say no?
